title: Open Questions
dek: What this archive does not know, ranked by how much finding out would change. Generated from this file rather than written by hand, so it cannot quietly fall a week behind the work.
lead:
Every question here names **what would settle it** and **which register holds the attempts**, because a question without either is a wish. A null result is still a result and it stops the next reader repeating the search — the attempts live in [what has been read](/searched/), the things only a person can do in [the errands](/errands/), and what this archive got wrong in [the corrections](/corrections/).

This page was 405 lines of hand-written prose until 15 September 2026. It had gone a day stale without anything being able to notice, which is the reason it is now generated.

open: live, and something could be done about it
blocked: waiting on a person, a fee, or somebody else's website
answered: settled, and kept because the answer is the finding

rows.rank: The join that decides the whole pedigree
rows.settles: PROB 11/1728/64 — his own will, proved 4 July 1827, digitised and free behind a free TNA sign-in. Seventy-one of the direct line's ancestors and twelve of its generations hang on the join immediately above him, and nothing else in his life names a father. A will names family.
tried: His baptism, c. 1741–1761

Swept on FindMyPast across all English record sets with variants on. NOT FOUND. His burial is confirmed — St Mary, Chatham, 19 May 1827, aged 76 — which is where the famous «1751» comes from, and it names no father.
Connolly's Roll of Officers of the Corps of Royal Engineers
Entry 203, «D'Arcy, Robert, C.B.» — the full career and «Died at Chatham, 13 5 1827». Only two D'Arcys in the whole Roll, 1660–1898. IT RECORDS NO PARENTAGE: the Roll does not carry fathers.
The Woolwich cadet registers

RULED OUT. WO 149 begins in 1790 and is at Sandhurst, so it cannot hold a cadet of the early 1770s. The printed Records of the Royal Military Academy of 1851 and 1892 are institutional histories, not registers, and have been read in full.
The printed Army Lists, 1783 · 1802 · 1803, and the Royal Military Calendar of 1820
Read 15 September 2026. They give rank, seniority and station year by year — Second Lieutenant in 1783, Captain by 1802, Major in the army by 1803 — AND NOT ONE NAMES A PARENT.
The London Gazette, 1770–1830
Silent, and structurally so: the Ordnance gazetted no British engineer commission in 1774, 1775 or 1776. All twenty-two Darcy notices of 1770–89 are other men.
Board of Ordnance records — WO 47, WO 54

STILL THE BEST HOPE, and not reachable from here. Until 1855 the Royal Engineers answered to the Board of Ordnance and kept separate records; a cadet warrant or commission entry of 17 January 1776 would be in the Ordnance minutes. Errand 28 established the series is WO 54/240. A letter to the Royal Engineers Museum at Chatham is drafted and unsent.
rows.note: He has no entry in the Dictionary of National Biography — the DNB's «D'Arcy, Robert» is the 4th Earl of Holderness, whose will is **not** in the Prerogative Court, searched and empty.

rows.q: Where and when was Hannah Saniger baptised, and who were her parents?
rows.rank: The oldest live question on the site
rows.settles: Berkeley St Mary's parish register after 1677, at Gloucestershire Archives — and Dursley St James and Cam St George, where the surname is six times commoner.
tried: Where she was born — CLOSED
BERKELEY, GLOUCESTERSHIRE, stated in the 1851 census at Drivers Fields and matching the tree exactly. That question is answered; this one replaces it.
FreeREG's Berkeley transcript

Measured at parish level on 15 September 2026 with a SMITH control: 3 exact and 36 uncertain results, EVERY ONE BETWEEN 1653 AND 1677. It is a thirty-year seventeenth-century fragment, so it can test one Saniger generation of six and no more.
Her parents

Still only a tree's assertion — John Saniger and Lydia. The tree adds Lydia Jones, born 13 March 1770 at Wotton-under-Edge, parents William and Sarah, died 7 July 1851 at Berkeley. Every one of those is testable and the baptism at Wotton has been tested: FreeREG does not list the parish.
rows.note: The deepest line in this archive — six Saniger generations from 1654 to 1805 — rests on other people's family trees. One generation of the six now has a documented candidate and a father the archive never had, **Edward Sainger of Wanswell**.

rows.q: Where did John Saniger and Lydia marry, about 1797?
rows.rank: One marriage, and it names Lydia
rows.settles: The Berkeley marriage register, or the Gloucestershire Family History Society's volunteers.
tried: Gloucestershire Archives

ANSWERED, and they do not do lookups. Andrew Parry, Senior Archives Assistant, 14 September 2026: «I'm afraid we don't offer any kind of research service.» He named the Family History Society instead.
The letter to the Society
Drafted and sitting in notes/letters/. Mail from David's address is his to send.
rows.note: Lydia is named by no record this archive has seen. Her death IS now doubly indexed — Thornbury, September quarter 1851, local register 3 entry 265 and GRO volume 11 page 329 — so a certificate would at least give her age and her widowhood.

rows.q: How do the medieval Swonhungres connect to the Sanigers of Berkeley?
rows.rank: Raised by the work of 15 September, and the archive claims no answer
rows.settles: The manor court rolls of Awre — Gloucestershire Archives D2156/1–4, D421/M7, D3270/362 and D3270/363 — which run from 1387 to 1881 and record surrenders, admissions and the customary heir of every tenant who died.
tried: The Berkeley deeds

195 records found on 15 September under the medieval spellings. They carry the family in the Vale from the 1270s to 1428, with filiations, an heirship and a named female ancestor — and Smyth's main line ends in 1401 with a John who died without issue.
The archive's own Sanigers
Appear at Berkeley from 1601 — John Saniger, yeoman, in D2957/41/18.
Between them
TWO HUNDRED YEARS OF SILENCE. No descent has been shown and none is claimed. The name and the place are documented as one thing; the people are not joined.
rows.note: The nearer and more useful version of this question is smaller: from the eleven men of the 1608 muster to John Saniger who married Lydia about 1797. Nothing found on 15 September touches it.

rows.rank: A generation this archive has never had
rows.settles: The marriage certificate of James Sneyd and Ann Biddulph, Stoke St Peter 1842, ordered locally from Stoke-on-Trent against reference 31/03/214. It would name BOTH FATHERS and their trades.
tried: Four censuses at Well Street, Hanley
Give her as «Ann» and nothing else — Ann 41 in 1861, Ann 52 in 1871, Anne 61 in 1881.
The free Staffordshire BMD index
Named her. The marriage is 1842 at Stoke St Peter, and four Sneyd births carry Biddulph as the mother's maiden name.
rows.note: Identified from an index, not from a certificate. It rests on a surname, a maiden name repeated four times, the right district and four matching ages.

rows.q: What became of Catherine Sneyd, born Hanley 1845?
rows.rank: A child the archive did not know existed
rows.settles: The 1851 census for Well Street, Hanley, read directly rather than through an index; or a death registration at Stoke between 1845 and 1851.
tried: The Staffordshire BMD birth index
HAN/007/057 — Catherine Sneyd, 1845, Hanley, mother's maiden name Biddulph. Three of her four siblings match the Well Street household exactly.
Every census read here
She appears in none of them. She either did not reach 1851, or was elsewhere on both nights.

rows.q: What did the three Sussex sisters leave, and to whom?
rows.settles: IR 27/396 — the Estate Duty register at the National Archives, which would name executors and legatees, and so name living relatives at three dates.
tried: The GRO death index
All three found: Charlotte 1869 Brighton 2b 152, Jane 1875 2b 203, Catherine 1876 2b 164 — and Charlotte re-confirmed in FreeBMD on 15 September as the control for that index.
The 1851 census
HO107/1646 f.357 p.59 sch.172, 22 Western Cottages, Brighton.
rows.note: FreeCEN cannot help: it returns NOUGHT for ARCY in Sussex 1851 while this archive has the sisters in that very census. The piece is not transcribed. That was correction 30.

rows.q: Three institutions are between houses, and it is not a research problem
tried: The Commonwealth War Graves Commission
Has refused automated access twice.
The Australian War Memorial
Mid-migration; its search returns nothing for any query. Its documents were reached by direct URL instead.
NSW State Archives
Now Museums of History NSW, at a new domain, with the old index addresses dead — which is what stopped the search for George Pitt D'Arcy's 1849 probate.

rows.q: When was Robert D'Arcy first commissioned?
rows.rank: Closed, and it had been wrong on six pages
tried: Three printed Army Lists

17 JANUARY 1776. The lists of 1778, 1781 and 1783 all carry him in an intact ditto-chain — and the 1783 edition sets his name ROBERT D'ARCEY, with an e, which is why outside catalogues had never returned him.
What was wrong
Five pages said 1776 and a sixth said 1778, for weeks, and the page that was wrong was the one that sounded most authoritative. Correction 29; agree.py then found six more stale copies.

rows.q: How many spellings of the surname are in the 1608 muster?
tried: Gloucestershire Notes & Queries

THREE, not four. Reviewing Maclean's 1902 edition — the edition this archive read — the reviewer listed its misreadings: «Thus SAINGER SHOULD READ SANIGER.» So the man living in the hamlet the surname came from is John Saniger of Saniger, his name and his address the same word.
What this does not overturn
SAINGER is a real form of the name, 44 times in the Berkeley registers. It is simply not a 1608 one. Correction 31.

rows.q: Is Smyth's pedigree of the Swonhungers trustworthy?
rows.rank: Closed, from the deeds he was reading
tried: The Berkeley Castle deeds, in the Discovery catalogue

Yes, and better. BCM/A/1/56/29 of 1354 is the partition Smyth describes; BCM/A/1/24/184 of 1356 is the deed he transcribed, and the catalogue says so — «[Transcript: Smyth, iii. 380-1.]»; MS 3549/4 at Birmingham names William's wife Isabella, as Smyth does.
And it adds a generation
The 1356 inspeximus calls John Swonhungre «his father, son and heir of John Swonhungre» — so there is a John above the John the printed pedigree begins with.

close: **Eight questions are live and three are closed and kept.** Of the eight, four wait on a person rather than on searching — a free sign-in at Kew, a letter from David's own address, a local certificate fee, and three institutions finishing their migrations. The other four can be worked on tonight, and the work list says which of them is being worked on.
